module_title: Nobel Prizes - Venues, Technical Rules, Controversies, and Deep Statistics
introduction: Designed for UPSC, State PCS, and CGL Tier-2, this advanced module covers the intricate operational rules of the Nobel Foundation, distribution venues, posthumous controversies, and the ultimate trivia regarding multi-prize winners.

core_concepts.title: The Geography of the Awards (Oslo vs. Stockholm)
core_concepts.description: A critical distinction: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, Norway, by a committee chosen by the Norwegian Parliament. The other five prizes (Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, Economics) are awarded in Stockholm, Sweden.

core_concepts.title: The Official Name of the Economics Prize
core_concepts.description: Technically, it is not a 'Nobel Prize'. Its official title is the 'Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel'. It is funded by Sweden's central bank, not by Alfred Nobel's original will.

core_concepts.title: The Posthumous Rule
core_concepts.description: According to the statutes of the Nobel Foundation, a prize cannot be awarded posthumously (after death). This rule was strictly enforced in 1974. Only two people in history have ever won it posthumously: Erik Axel Karlfeldt (1931) and UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld (1961).

core_concepts.title: The Mahatma Gandhi Controversy
core_concepts.description: Widely considered the greatest omission in Nobel history, Mahatma Gandhi was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize five times (1937, 1938, 1939, 1947, and 1948) but was never awarded the prize.

core_concepts.title: The Sharing Rule
core_concepts.description: A single Nobel Prize can be divided among a maximum of three individuals in a given year. It cannot be split among four or more people.

important_entities.name: Linus Pauling
important_entities.significance: The ONLY person in history to win two unshared (solo) Nobel Prizes: Chemistry in 1954 and Peace in 1962.

important_entities.name: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)
important_entities.significance: The ICRC has won the Nobel Peace Prize three times (1917, 1944, and 1963), primarily for its humanitarian work during the World Wars.

important_entities.name: John B. Goodenough
important_entities.significance: Won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (2019) at the age of 97 for his work in developing lithium-ion batteries.

important_entities.name: The Curie Family
important_entities.significance: The Curie family holds the record for the most Nobels. Marie (2), her husband Pierre (1), their daughter Irène Joliot-Curie (1), and their son-in-law Frédéric Joliot (1) have collectively won 5 Nobel Prizes.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If an examiner asks, 'Where are the Nobel Prizes distributed?', do not blindly tick 'Stockholm'. Look for the word 'Peace'. If it's the Peace prize, the answer is exclusively 'Oslo, Norway'.
While Marie Curie won two Nobels, she shared her 1903 Physics prize with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. Linus Pauling is the only individual to have won two Nobels completely solo.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Associate the 'Peace' prize exclusively with the distinct city of 'Oslo'.

exam_strategy_tips: In advanced statement-based questions, examiners will test your knowledge of the 'Posthumous Rule' or the 'Maximum of 3 people' rule. Remember that since 1974, nobody can be deliberately awarded the prize if they are already dead at the time of the announcement.
